name: Sam Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Sam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We've got no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. This conversation is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a new housing estate on the edge of town, two hundred and twenty homes, for one of the big house builders. I'm a junior site carpenter, so it's first fix mostly: stud walls, fitting the roof trusses when the crane drops them, stairs, door linings. We do one plot, then the next plot, then the next, all nearly the same house. My chargehand, Lewis, gives me the easy plots because I'm still slow on stairs.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the lads and I like that the money's decent now I'm past my first year. What wears me out is doing the same house forty times and the travel, it's forty minutes each way in traffic. The funny bit is me and Ella, she's a dental nurse, are saving to buy one of these exact houses one day. I've fitted the stairs in a house I can't afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, glad that's sorted, and get on with it. Maybe a joke in the group chat about the robot uprising being cancelled. I don't really do strong opinions on stuff like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Means we stay on track. Keep saving, maybe get our deposit together in three or four years, get one of these houses. I'd keep learning, get quicker on stairs, maybe chargehand by my mid thirties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing. We've got about five months of bills saved, separate from the bit for the deposit, and I'd keep adding to both. I use the AI app now and then to work out a tricky stair calculation, and I'd carry on with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, fine. Bit of relief, like when a big match ends in a boring draw and nobody gets hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI for stair calculations. How did that start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One of the lads, Jordan, showed me. I'd been stuck on a winder, that's a stair that turns a corner, and Lewis was busy. Jordan typed it in and it gave the rise and going, and it was right, so now I check things with it now and then. Wouldn't trust it on its own, mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, is there anything you'd still want to change yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The travel, honestly. If one of the firms nearer home took me on, I'd go. And I'd like to do a few weekend jobs, fitting doors for neighbours, to speed up the deposit.

S0.say: I'd say fair enough, glad that's sorted, and maybe joke in the group chat about the robot uprising being cancelled. I don't really do strong opinions on things like that.
S0.think: Privately it means he and Ella stay on track to buy a house in three or four years. He'd keep improving and aim to be a chargehand by his mid thirties.
S0.do: Keeps working on the estate and adds to both his five months of savings and the house deposit. Keeps using an AI app now and then to check stair calculations.
S0.feel: Calm, with a bit of relief, like a boring draw where nobody gets hurt.
S0.quote: Bit of relief, like when a big match ends in a boring draw and nobody gets hurt.
S0.fieldNote: Sam is easy-going and centred on a single concrete goal: buying a house like the ones he builds. He uses AI casually, after a colleague showed him, and checks its answers. Nothing in this picture threatens his plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say things change, it's not the end of the world. Learn what you need to and keep going. Probably what my dad would say too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think house building is one of the places they'll go for. Every house on our estate is the same, so a factory could make the walls and roofs and we'd just bolt them together. They already do some of that on other sites. That'd mean fewer of us, and juniors go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what Lewis and the older lads do, and if they start going on courses for the factory panels, I'd go too. I'd use the AI app more for setting out, since I'd be behind otherwise. And I'd slow down on the deposit a bit, keep more in the bills pot, maybe get to six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a noise in the van you hope is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said juniors go first. Have you seen that happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter, when sales slowed, they let two juniors go on the plot next to ours. Lewis kept me because I turn up on time, he said, which isn't exactly a skill. So yeah, I know where I stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ella think about slowing down the deposit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be annoyed but she'd get it. Her job's safer than mine, I reckon, nobody wants a robot in their mouth. She'd probably say keep going with the deposit and stop overthinking.

S1.say: I'd say things change, it's not the end of the world, so learn what you need and keep going. That's probably what my dad would say too.
S1.think: Privately he thinks volume house building will be targeted, with walls and roofs made in factories and fewer site carpenters. Juniors would go first.
S1.do: Follows his chargehand and older colleagues onto any factory-panel courses and uses the AI app more for setting out. Shifts money from the house deposit into his bills cushion to reach six months.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a noise in the van you hope is nothing.
S1.quote: Lewis kept me because I turn up on time, he said, which isn't exactly a skill.
S1.fieldNote: His public line is relaxed and his private one is sharper, shaped by seeing juniors laid off last winter. He'd follow the older hands rather than lead. The house deposit is the first thing he'd quietly slow down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, mate, nobody saw that coming, we'll all have to work it out together. I'd probably say the government needs to sort something, but I don't know what. I wouldn't be ranting online, that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think that's me done as a carpenter. Two years and a robot can fit trusses and stairs? I'd be twenty-nine, no school certificates, two years of first fix. That's nothing to bargain with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can. Keep in mind there are only about 2 years before it arrives.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, Ella and I would stop saving for the house and keep the money as a cushion, there's no point buying a house if you can't pay the mortgage in two years. I'd keep working as long as there's work, and watch what other people do before I jump. If anyone I know got work running or fixing the machines, I'd ask them how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. That's the word. Like being on a roof when the wind picks up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So the house plan stops completely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, completely. That's the bit that'd hurt most, honestly, more than the job. We've been saving three years, and the plan was a house before thirty-two, maybe a kid after that. It'd all go on hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd watch what others do before jumping. With only two years, is that enough time to wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, no. You've caught me there. I suppose I'd give it six months, and if nobody's worked it out by then, I'd have to try something myself.

S2.say: I'd say nobody saw that coming and we'll all have to work it out together, and that the government needs to sort something. I wouldn't rant online.
S2.think: Privately he thinks he's done as a carpenter: at twenty-nine, without school certificates and with two years of first fix, he has nothing to bargain with.
S2.do: Stops saving for the house and keeps the money as a cushion with Ella. Keeps working while there is work and watches others for about six months before trying something himself, asking anyone who gets work fixing the machines.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like being on a roof when the wind picks up.
S2.quote: There's no point buying a house if you can't pay the mortgage in two years.
S2.fieldNote: For Sam the job loss matters less than losing the house plan, and with it the idea of a child after thirty-two. When challenged on waiting with only two years, he conceded and set himself a six-month limit. His steady habit of following others feels risky here and he knows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you're sensible. Don't panic, make a plan. I'd probably say that to the lads at football on a Thursday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years puts me at thirty-two. I'd want to be on the right side of it by then, maybe not as a carpenter but doing something on the site, like site manager, checking the machines did it right. Lewis says someone's always got to sign things off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can. This time there are about 5 years of warning.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, keep working and look into a site supervision course, the kind the firm sometimes pays for. Ella and I would keep saving but maybe buy a smaller flat instead of a house, so the mortgage is something one of us could cover. By year three I'd want to have the course done and be trying for an assistant site manager job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's manageable. I can see a way through if I don't sit on my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why site manager and not something else completely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I know sites and I like people. I wouldn't be good at an office job, but I can talk to a crane driver and an electrician and a client in the same hour. If the robots need someone to boss them about, that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know when to start the course? You said earlier you like to wait and see.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the firm offers it to more than a couple of people, that's my sign. If they're paying to train us, they know something's coming. I'd want to be in the first group, not the last.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you're sensible, so don't panic and make a plan. I'd say that to the lads at Thursday football.
S3.think: Privately he wants to be on the right side of it by thirty-two, perhaps as a site manager who checks the machines' work. Someone always has to sign things off.
S3.do: Keeps working and takes a site supervision course, ideally one the firm pays for, aiming for an assistant site manager job by year three. Keeps saving with Ella but plans a smaller flat with a mortgage one of them could cover.
S3.feel: Anxious but manageable, seeing a way through if he acts.
S3.quote: If the robots need someone to boss them about, that's me.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Sam's steady style into a plan with a trigger: when the firm offers training widely, he goes. He sees his strength as dealing with people on site, not technical skill. The housing plan shrinks from a house to a flat rather than disappearing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is ages, loads of time to sort ourselves out. Probably I'd say that's a problem for the next government, half joking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's a relief compared with the other two. I'd get a proper run at carpentry, maybe chargehand, and still have time to move into site management before it lands. I'd be thirty-seven, so still young enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can. This time there are about 10 years of warning.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, nothing big changes. We'd keep saving and probably still buy the house in three or four years, because we'd have years of wages to pay it down. Around year four or five, when I see the robots arriving on other sites, I'd do the site supervision course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only a bit. It's in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd still buy the house, even knowing it's coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so. Ten years is long enough that we'd be a good way into the mortgage, and Ella's job is steadier. If we wait for a perfect future we'll be renting forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make you speed up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Lewis started looking at other jobs. He's my weather vane, he's been in the game twenty years. If he jumps, I jump.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is ages and loads of time to sort ourselves out, and half joke that it's a problem for the next government.
S4.think: Privately it's a relief compared with the faster pictures: he gets a proper run at carpentry and time to move into site management. At thirty-seven he'd still be young enough.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving, and still plans to buy the house with Ella in three or four years. Takes a site supervision course around year four or five, or sooner if his chargehand changes jobs.
S4.feel: Slightly uneasy, with the worry in the background.
S4.quote: If we wait for a perfect future we'll be renting forever.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Sam's house plan returns intact, and he reasons it out in terms of years of mortgage paid down. His chargehand Lewis is his 'weather vane' for when to act. He uses humour to keep the subject at arm's length.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question, because the house plan dies and I've got nothing to switch to. What would help is the firms paying for site courses early and telling us honestly what's coming, so we're not finding out when the van doesn't pick us up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to house prices. If robots build them cheaper, maybe me and Ella could finally afford one, even if I'm not the one building it. That'd be a strange kind of win.

headlineQuote: If robots build them cheaper, maybe me and Ella could finally afford one, even if I'm not the one building it.
portrait: Sam Novak is a 27-year-old junior site carpenter on a big housing estate, fitting trusses and stairs in houses he and his girlfriend Ella, a dental nurse, are saving to buy. He's easy-going, avoids strong opinions, and uses AI now and then after a colleague showed him. Calm if AI fizzles and uneasy with steady change, he's alarmed by AGI in two years mainly because the house plan would stop. With five or ten years he plans to move into site supervision, using his chargehand Lewis as his signal for when to move.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because the house plan would end and he'd have nothing to switch to.
whatWouldHelp: Firms paying for site supervision courses early and telling workers honestly what's coming.
